stimulus.text:
The Treaty of Paris, signed February 10, 1763, ended the Seven Years' War. Its terms for North America were:

| Territory | 1763 outcome |
| Canada and all French land east of the Mississippi | To Britain |
| Louisiana west of the Mississippi | To Spain |
| Florida | To Britain, from Spain |
| Guadeloupe and Martinique | Returned to France |
| Saint Pierre and Miquelon | Kept by France, with Newfoundland fishing rights |
stimulus.source_note: Terms of the Treaty of Paris (February 10, 1763); France's choice between Canada and the sugar islands is recorded in the treaty history.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Terms of the Treaty of Paris (February 10, 1763); France's choice between Canada and the sugar islands is recorded in the treaty history.
stem: Based on the table, which of the following best explains France's decision to give up Canada while keeping its Caribbean sugar islands?

options.text: French ministers judged the sugar islands worth more than Canada's fur trade, and Canada would have been costly to defend.

options.misconception: France had valued Canada for a century — it was the heart of New France — and gave it up only after losing the war.
options.text: France had no interest in North America and gave up Canada because it had never valued the territory.

options.misconception: France did negotiate: it kept the sugar islands and its fishing rights, and chose which territory to surrender.
options.text: Britain demanded Canada as the price of peace, and France had no choice but to accept every British demand.

options.misconception: France gave Louisiana to Spain, not to Britain, and received nothing in exchange for it in the Treaty of Paris.
options.text: France traded Canada for Louisiana because it wanted to keep a North American empire centered on the Mississippi.

rationales.A: The table shows the trade: France lost Canada and the lands east of the Mississippi, but kept Guadeloupe and Martinique — Background: France also kept Saint Lucia. Choiseul and Voltaire both said the choice was deliberate — sugar revenues outweighed the fur trade — and Canada, already conquered by British troops, would have cost a fortune to reconquer and hold. France kept the profitable islands and let the expensive continent go.
rationales.B: France had built Canada over a century and fought hard to keep it; losing it was a defeat, not indifference.
rationales.C: Britain did offer France a choice between Canada and the sugar islands, and France chose — the table shows what it kept.
rationales.D: Louisiana went to Spain by a separate agreement, and France got nothing for it; the Canada-for-sugar-islands exchange is the one the table records.
rationales.general:
1. Read the table's two columns. France loses Canada and the east of the Mississippi; it keeps Guadeloupe and Martinique. Background: France also kept Saint Lucia.
2. Ask what each side was worth. The sugar islands poured revenue into France; Canada's fur trade was thin by comparison.
3. Ask what holding Canada would cost. A vast territory already occupied by British troops, far from France, against a Britain that had just proved it could take it.
Remember: empires keep what pays and drop what costs — and France's choice tells you what it thought its empire was for.
